extracted.intended_audience: owners/operators of electric generating units (EGUs), industry stakeholders, environmental consultants, and regulators
extracted.subtask_description: Regulatory requirements and Agency determinations for New Source Performance Standards (NSPS) for new, modified, and reconstructed stationary combustion turbines and fossil fuel-fired steam generating units, including BSER, emissions limits, monitoring, reporting, compliance dates, and extension procedures. Focuses on Phase 1 and Phase 2 standards (including CCS), measurement approaches, recordkeeping, and treatment of startups/shutdowns/malfunctions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intermediate-load combustion turbine standard of performance (Phase 1)
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA is finalizing a standard of 1,170 lb CO2/MWh-gross for intermediate load combustion turbines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This standard is based on demonstrated performance by multiple turbine designs, has been shown by a frame simple turbine and by efficient versions of LMS100 and SGT‑A65 installations; EPA considered but rejected 1,190 lb CO2/MWh-gross because it would not represent the BSER. EPA finds the standard achievable with proper maintenance, across multiple manufacturers, with and without intercooling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phase-2 standard for base-load combustion turbines (90% CCS)
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA proposed and is finalizing that 90 percent CCS (as part of the CCS pathway) qualifies as the second component of the BSER for base load combustion turbines, and reduced the emissions rate by 89 percent to determine the CCS-based phase-2 standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The CCS percent reduction is based on a CCS system capturing 90 percent of the emitting CO2 being operational anytime the combustion turbine is operating. EPA adjusted the standard for uncontrolled emission rates of fuels relative to natural gas (e.g., 100% distillate oil-fired turbines would have 120 lb CO2/MWh‑gross). EPA solicited comment on a 75–90% reduction range and on potential availability/reliability/startup timing differences between CCS and the turbine; EPA determined 90% CCS has been demonstrated and is appropriate for base load turbines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of reconstructed stationary combustion turbines (BSER equivalence and feasibility exemption)
rubrics_metrics.description: The BSER is the same for new and reconstructed stationary combustion turbines; reconstructed turbines would be able to use available upgrade packages to comply with intermediate load emission standards. A reconstructed turbine is not required to meet the standards if doing so is deemed to be 'technologically and economically' infeasible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA used the same emissions analysis for new and reconstructed turbines. Examples of retrofit/upgrades that can enable compliance include GE's Advanced Gas Path, Siemens' Hot Start on the Fly, Solar Turbines' compressor restaging, steam injection (estimated retrofit equipment cost $250/kW), and conversion to combined cycle via HRSG. For CCS retrofit cost-estimating, EPA approximates increasing capture capital costs by 9% and decreasing net efficiency by 0.3%, producing compliance cost estimates (e.g., $17/MWh and $51/ton for certain H-Class turbines). The technological/economic infeasibility determination is case-by-case and considers the identified BSER as well as other technologies EPA reviewed; site-specific feasibility could allow other technically feasible and reasonably‑costed options to meet reconstructed standards. Equipment upgrades and best operating practices could in some cases achieve sufficient reductions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modification definition and treatment for combustion turbines
rubrics_metrics.description: CAA section 111(a)(4) defines 'modification' as any physical change or change in method of operation that either increases the amount of any air pollutant emitted or results in emission of any pollutant not previously emitted; certain changes are exempt under 40 CFR 60.2 and 60.14(e).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA did not propose or solicit comment on standards of performance for modifications of combustion turbines in this rule and is not establishing any standards for modifications in this final rule, based on limited evidence that owners/operators will undertake NSPS modifications and limited information about such modifications' frequency and feasibility. (In 2015 EPA had delayed establishing modification standards for similar reasons.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards apply at all times; no alternate SSM standards
rubrics_metrics.description: All standards in subpart TTTTa apply at all times, including periods of startup and shutdown; EPA is not establishing alternate standards for those periods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA follows Sierra Club v. EPA (D.C. Cir.) reasoning that continuous standards are required; NSPS general provisions would apply unless specifically overridden. EPA's analysis used CEMS data that includes all periods of operation, so startup, shutdown, and malfunction periods were not excluded. EPA distinguishes routine, predictable startup/shutdown from malfunctions (sudden, infrequent, not reasonably preventable). EPA interprets CAA section 111 as not requiring malfunctions to be factored into setting the standard of performance; caselaw (e.g., U.S. Sugar Corp. v. EPA) supports this approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allowed approaches to determine CO2 emissions (testing/monitoring methods)
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA allows three approaches for determining CO2 emissions: (1) a CO2 CEMS and stack gas flow monitor; (2) hourly heat input, fuel characteristics, and F factors for EGUs firing oil or gas; or (3) Tier 3 calculations using fuel use and carbon content (GHGRP approach).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The first two approaches are used under the Acid Rain program (40 CFR part 75), and the Tier 3 approach is used under GHGRP (40 CFR part 98, subpart C). EPA believes using approaches already in use is cost-effective. ECMPS reporting expects hourly/daily CO2 values and contains checks to validate data; ECMPS does not currently accommodate GHGRP Tier 3. EPA requested comment on whether continuous CO2 CEMS and stack gas flow should be the sole compliance method, noted an estimated annualized cost (~$52,000) to adopt CEMS/flow where none exist, and ultimately allows the heat-input/factor approach as an alternative for oil/gas EGUs. Each CO2 CEMS and flow monitor must undergo regular QA/QC including periodic relative accuracy test audits (comparison to independent monitor). EPA disagrees that part 75 data requirements are punitive or systematically biased.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitoring and reporting requirements for sources implementing CCS
rubrics_metrics.description: If an affected unit employs CCS and injects CO2 underground, it must report under GHGRP subpart RR or VV; if the emitting EGU sends captured CO2 offsite, it must transfer CO2 to a facility that reports under GHGRP subpart RR or VV.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compliance with the standard is determined exclusively by the tons of CO2 captured by the emitting EGU; tons sequestered by the geologic sequestration site are not part of the emitting EGU's compliance calculation. EPA leverages GHGRP reporting to verify transfer to geologic sequestration sites and to avoid duplicative MRV. The final rule does not regulate downstream recipients of captured CO2—regulatory obligations apply exclusively to the emitting EGU; existing UIC and geologic sequestration regulatory requirements remain separate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recordkeeping and reporting via ECMPS (quarterly reports)
rubrics_metrics.description: EGU owners/operators must prepare and submit reports in accordance with the Acid Rain Program's ECMPS (quarterly). Existing recordkeeping requirements at 40 CFR part 60.5560, general provisions (60.7(b), (f)), and subpart F of part 75 are retained in new subpart TTTTa.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA expects all EGUs to be familiar with ECMPS, minimizing additional cost or burden; if an EGU is not already covered by ECMPS, estimated annual per-unit cost would be about $8,500. EPA is retaining explicit lists of required items (data and calculations) and maintaining annual recordkeeping cost equivalence with prior subpart TTTT requirements. EPA is finalizing a specific requirement that owners/operators maintain records of electric sales to demonstrate they did not sell electricity above the threshold triggering the output-based standard (for units subject to a heat-input based standard).

rubrics_metrics.name: Compliance dates for new/reconstructed affected sources
rubrics_metrics.description: Owners/operators of affected sources that commenced construction or reconstruction after May 23, 2023 must meet the requirements of 40 CFR part 60, subpart TTTTa upon startup of the new or reconstructed affected facility or the effective date of the final rule, whichever is later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This compliance schedule is consistent with section 111 of the CAA and with EPA's determinations about achievable timelines for installation/startup of BSER technologies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phase 2 compliance date extension (up to 1 year) — eligibility and documentation
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA will allow owners/operators of new or reconstructed base load stationary combustion turbine EGUs to request a limited Phase 2 compliance extension of up to 1 year (to January 1, 2033) based on a case-by-case demonstration of necessity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The mechanism is only for unavoidable delays in installation/startup of controls (not for reassessing compliance strategy). Requests must be received at least 180 days before January 1, 2032, and must document circumstances entirely beyond the owner's/operator's control and that all possible steps to install/start up controls have been taken. Acceptable circumstances include delays related to permitting, delivery or construction of parts, or development of necessary infrastructure (e.g., CO2 pipelines). Documentation may include vendor or engineering firm statements, permit delay records, or infrastructure construction/permitting records. If granted and the source still cannot install/start controls by January 1, 2033, the source may adjust operation to the intermediate load subcategory (12-month capacity factor between 20–40%) and must then comply with intermediate-load standards until controls are operational.

rubrics_metrics.name: Withdrawal of 2018 Proposal re: BSER for coal-fired steam generating units
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA is withdrawing the 2018 Proposal that would have found 'highly efficient generation technology combined with best operating practices' to be the BSER for coal-fired steam generating units.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA now concludes CCS technology is adequately demonstrated for coal-fired steam generating units and therefore it is not appropriate to impose the less effective control. EPA is considering whether to revise the 2015 Rule to account for CCS improvements and tax credits under the IRA. For technical rationale, EPA directs readers to the docket technical memorandum '2018 Proposal Withdrawal.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'large modification' and standards for modified steam generating units
rubrics_metrics.description: In the 2015 NSPS, a 'large modification' is defined as a physical change or change in method of operation that results in an increase in hourly CO2 emissions of more than 10 percent when compared to the source's highest hourly emissions in the previous 5 years; such a modified unit is required to meet a unit-specific CO2 emission limit determined by that unit's best demonstrated historical performance (2002 to time of modification).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 2015 NSPS did not include standards for 'small modifications' (≤10% increase). EPA concluded limited historical notifications of NSPS modifications justified promulgating standards for larger modifications but not for all types of modifications at this time due to insufficient information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial and technical amendments to regulatory text and compliance flexibilities
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA is finalizing several less significant amendments: defining acronyms when first used, adding SI equivalents for heat-input-based standards, correcting cross-references, updating ANSI/ASME/ASTM test method versions, and adding compliance flexibilities for EGUs sharing a common generator or common stack.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA is also finalizing an explicit requirement that owners/operators maintain records of electric sales to demonstrate non-applicability of output-based standards and is incorporating these editorial/technical amendments into subpart TTTTa (see redline strikeout rule version in docket). These amendments are intended to be editorial or to add compliance flexibility without changing substantive requirements.
